title: For Such a Time as This
subtitle: Esther in Poems & Pictures
author: Timothy Holt
beforeYouBegin:
Esther begins with a banquet that lasts half a year and ends with neighbors carrying plates of food to one another's doors. In between: an orphan girl raised by her cousin, a jar of myrrh, a man who will not bow, a lot cast for a day of ruin, three days of fasting, a golden scepter held out, a king who cannot sleep, and a book of records opened to exactly the right page.

This book walks through it in thirty-two short poems, in four parts. Each poem sits beside a picture and under a single line of Scripture. The name of God is never written in the book of Esther, and the poems try to notice where his hand is hidden anyway. The pictures stay with the things the story touches—a signet ring, a sleepless lamp, a table set for three —and leave the faces to your imagination.

The poems are not the Bible. They are one reader's response to it. Open the book of Esther alongside this book, and let the real words have the last word.

paintings.title: one hundred eighty days
paintings.epigraph: “He displayed the riches of his glorious kingdom and the honor of his excellent majesty many days”
paintings.poem:
half a year
of showing off.

white and blue hangings,
silver rings,
couches of gold
on a floor of colored stone,
wine poured
from cups no two alike.

every name in the empire
was spoken in that garden
except one.

the story never says it.
keep reading anyway.
he is there.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “one hundred eighty days” (Esther 1:4–7)—where the poem notes, “keep reading anyway. he is there”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the queen who would not come
paintings.epigraph: “But the queen V ashti refused to come at the king’s commandment”
paintings.poem:
seven days of wine,
and the king sent for her
to be looked at.

she said no.

the whole empire
wrote a law about it,
and she walks out
of the story
without another word.

but a door
has been left open
in the palace,

and someone
no one has heard of yet
is on her way.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the queen who would not come” (Esther 1:10–12)—where the poem notes, “no one has heard of yet is on her way”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: myrtle
paintings.epigraph: “for she had neither father nor mother.”
paintings.poem:
no father.
no mother.
a long way from Jerusalem.

just a cousin
who took her in
and called her daughter.

she had two names,
one for the empire
and one for home.

God is like that
in this book too:
unnamed,
and caring for her
all the same.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “myrtle” (Esther 2:5–7)—where the poem notes, “and caring for her all the same”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: every day by the court
paintings.epigraph: “Mordecai walked every day in front of the court of the women’s house, to find out how Esther was doing”
paintings.poem:
he couldn't go in.
he could only walk past.

every day
the same wall,
the same gate,
the same question:
how is she?

some love
can only stand outside
and ask.

it still counts.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “every day by the court” (Esther 2:11)—where the poem notes, “it still counts”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: twelve months of myrrh
paintings.epigraph: “six months with oil of myrrh, and six months with sweet fragrances”
paintings.poem:
a whole year
of oil and perfume
before one evening
with the king.

she was being made ready
for a crown.

she didn't know
she was also being made ready
for a day
when she would have to
walk in uninvited.

the long waiting
is never
only waiting.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In the quiet after the noise, what gentle truth from Esther 2:12 (“is never only waiting”) is asking for your unhurried attention today?

paintings.title: she required nothing
paintings.epigraph: “she required nothing but what Hegai the king’s eunuch, the keeper of the women, advised.”
paintings.poem:
she could have asked
for anything to take with her:
jewels, silk, gold.

she asked for nothing
but good advice.

and the girl
who reached for nothing
was handed a crown.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “she required nothing” (Esther 2:15–17)—where the poem notes, “who reached for nothing was handed a crown”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: written in the book
paintings.epigraph: “it was written in the book of the chronicles in the king’s presence.”
paintings.poem:
a whisper at the gate.
a plot against the king.
Mordecai heard it
and told.

the matter was settled,
a scribe wrote it down,
and the scroll went on a shelf.

no reward.
no thank you.

just a line
in a book no one reads.

hold on to that line.
it will be read aloud
on exactly the right night.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In the quiet after the noise, what gentle truth from Esther 2:21–23 (“it will be read aloud on exactly the right night”) is asking for your unhurried attention today?

paintings.title: he would not bow
paintings.epigraph: “But Mordecai didn’t bow down or pay him homage.”
paintings.poem:
everyone at the gate
bent low
when Haman walked by.

one man
stayed standing.

they asked him why,
day after day.

his answer
was only this:
i am a Jew.

some knees
are already
spoken for.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “he would not bow” (Esther 3:2–4)—where the poem notes, “are already spoken for”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the lot
paintings.epigraph: “they cast Pur, that is, the lot”
paintings.poem:
Haman let chance
choose the day.

day after day
the lots rolled,
month after month,

until they stopped
on the twelfth month,
almost a year away.

he thought
he was picking a date.

he was giving
the other side
almost a year.

another book says
the lot is cast into the lap,
but the answer
comes from the Lord.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the lot” (Esther 3:7)—where the poem notes, “but the answer comes from the Lord”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the ring
paintings.epigraph: “The king took his ring from his hand, and gave it to Haman”
paintings.poem:
a ring slid off one finger
and onto another.

that was all it took.

no one asked
who the people were
or what they had done.

a signet ring
has no conscience.
it only presses
what it's told.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the ring” (Esther 3:10–11)—where the poem notes, “it only presses what it's told”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the city was perplexed
paintings.epigraph: “The king and Haman sat down to drink; but the city of Susa was perplexed.”
paintings.poem:
in the palace,
two men raised their cups.

in the streets,
a whole city
stood reading the notice
and could not make sense of it.

the powerful
are often
the last to notice
what they have done.

the city
knew something was wrong.

so did heaven.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the city was perplexed” (Esther 3:15)—where the poem notes, “so did heaven”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: sackcloth
paintings.epigraph: “Mordecai tore his clothes, and put on sackcloth with ashes”
paintings.poem:
he tore his clothes
and walked into the middle of the city
and cried out loud.

they don't let sackcloth
through the king's gate.

but grief
has other doors.

in every province
where the letter came,
people lay down in ashes
and did not eat.

the book does not say
who they were crying to.

it doesn't have to.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “sackcloth” (Esther 4:1–3)—where the poem notes, “it doesn't have to”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: thirty days
paintings.epigraph: “I have not been called to come in to the king these thirty days.”
paintings.poem:
queen,
and still afraid
of a door.

thirty days
without a word from him.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: What anxious weight can you place into the hands of the One who says, “Be still” and walks beside you in Esther 4:11?

paintings.title: from another place
paintings.epigraph: “relief and deliverance will come to the Jews from another place”
paintings.poem:
if you stay quiet,
Mordecai said,
help will still come.
from another place.

he didn't say
whose place.

he didn't need to.

the rescue
was never
riding on her.

the question was only
whether she would
be part of it.

who knows?
maybe this is why
you are where you are.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “from another place” (Esther 4:13–14)—where the poem notes, “maybe this is why you are where you are”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the fast
paintings.epigraph: “fast for me, and neither eat nor drink three days, night or day.”
paintings.poem:
before the queen
went in to the king,
a whole city
went without bread.

three days.
three nights.
no food, no water.

and the maidens in the palace
did the same.

nobody wrote down the prayers.

but an empty bowl
is a kind of prayer,

and so many empty bowls
across one city
make a sound
heaven can hear.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the fast” (Esther 4:16)—where the poem notes, “make a sound heaven can hear”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: if I perish
paintings.epigraph: “if I perish, I perish.”
paintings.poem:
she did not say
i will not perish.

she said
i am going in.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “if I perish” (Esther 4:16)—where the poem notes, “she said i am going in”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the third day
paintings.epigraph: “Now on the third day, Esther put on her royal clothing”
paintings.poem:
on the third day
she put the robe back on.

three days hungry.
three days praying.
and now the purple
and the crown.

she did not walk in
as a beggar.

she walked in
as who she was,

and let the fasting
be the part
no one could see.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the third day” (Esther 5:1)—where the poem notes, “be the part no one could see”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the golden scepter
paintings.epigraph: “the king held out to Esther the golden scepter that was in his hand.”
paintings.poem:
the law said
one of two things
would happen.

she stood in the court
and waited
to find out which.

and the king
held out the gold.

she came near
and touched the tip.

that is all.
a hand stretched out,
and another hand
reaching back.

you can build
a whole faith
on a moment like that.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In the quiet after the noise, what gentle truth from Esther 5:2 (“a whole faith on a moment like that”) is asking for your unhurried attention today?

paintings.title: a table for three
paintings.epigraph: “let the king and Haman come today to the banquet that I have prepared for him.”
paintings.poem:
up to half the kingdom,
he said.

she asked for dinner.

and at dinner,
asked for dinner again.

she was not afraid
to be slow.

some things
are not rushed
into the open.

they are served
in their time.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: What anxious weight can you place into the hands of the One who says, “Be still” and walks beside you in Esther 5:4?

paintings.title: all this avails me nothing
paintings.epigraph: “Y et all this avails me nothing, so long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king’s gate.”
paintings.poem:
riches.
sons.
promotions.
dinner with the queen.

he counted every one
out loud.

and then said
none of it mattered
because one man
would not stand up.

a heart like that
could own the whole empire
and still be hungry.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “all this avails me nothing” (Esther 5:11–13)—where the poem notes, “could own the whole empire and still be hungry”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the sleepless king
paintings.epigraph: “He commanded the book of records of the chronicles to be brought, and they were read to the king.”
paintings.poem:
that night
the most powerful man in the world
could not sleep.

nothing unusual.
kings lie awake.

so he did
what tired men do
and asked for something dull
to be read to him.

the story doesn't say
who kept him up.

it just leaves
the lamp on.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the sleepless king” (Esther 6:1)—where the poem notes, “it just leaves the lamp on”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: nothing has been done
paintings.epigraph: ““Nothing has been done for him.””
paintings.poem:
out of all those scrolls,
all those years,
the reader stopped
on one line:

Mordecai.
the plot at the gate.

and the king asked,
what did we do for him?

nothing.

good done in secret
can sit on a shelf
a long time.

it is not lost.
it is waiting
for the right night.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In the quiet after the noise, what gentle truth from Esther 6:2–3 (“it is waiting for the right night”) is asking for your unhurried attention today?

paintings.title: the man the king delights to honor
paintings.epigraph: “Thus it shall be done to the man whom the king delights to honor!”
paintings.poem:
who could the king
want to honor
more than me?
Haman thought.

so he described
the robe,
the horse,
the crown,
the parade.

and then was told
to lead the horse himself
and call out the words

for Mordecai.

he walked home
with his head covered.

the one who had stayed standing
rode.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: What single step right in front of you is already lit by His word today, even if the far horizon remains unseen (Esther 6:6–11)?

paintings.title: my people
paintings.epigraph: “let my life be given me at my petition, and my people at my request.”
paintings.poem:
the second banquet.
the same question.
what do you want?

this time she said it:
my life,
and my people.

for years
she had kept quiet
about who she was.

now she said it
in front of the man
who wanted them gone.

hiding had kept her safe.
telling the truth
kept them alive.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “my people” (Esther 7:3–4)—where the poem notes, “telling the truth kept them alive”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the one he built
paintings.epigraph: “Then the king’s wrath was pacified.”
paintings.poem:
the thing Haman had built
for Mordecai
was the thing
that ended him.

the story says it
in one short line
and doesn't stay to watch.

neither will we.

a pit dug for someone else
has a way
of keeping its digger.

and the king's anger
went quiet.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the one he built” (Esther 7:9–10)—where the poem notes, “and the king's anger went quiet”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the ring again
paintings.epigraph: “The king took off his ring, which he had taken from Haman, and gave it to Mordecai.”
paintings.poem:
the same ring.
the same king.

a few chapters ago
it sealed a death sentence.

now it rests
on the hand
of the man
it was meant to erase.

the old seal
could not be broken.

so a new one
was pressed
beside it.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the ring again” (Esther 8:2)—where the poem notes, “was pressed beside it”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: how can I endure
paintings.epigraph: “For how can I endure to see the evil that would come to my people?”
paintings.poem:
Haman was gone,
and she had a house,
and she was safe.

it would have been easy
to stop there.

she fell down
at the king's feet again
and wept.

she could not
be happy alone.

and the scepter
came out a second time.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “how can I endure” (Esther 8:3–6)—where the poem notes, “and the scepter came out a second time”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: swift horses
paintings.epigraph: “sent letters by courier on horseback, riding on royal horses that were bred from swift steeds.”
paintings.poem:
the first letter
could not be taken back.
Persian law.

so a second letter
went out after it,
faster,
on the king's best horses,

every province,
every language,
every road:

you may stand
and defend your lives.

the first word
was still written.

it just wasn't
the last word anymore.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “swift horses” (Esther 8:10–14)—where the poem notes, “it just wasn't the last word anymore”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: light and gladness
paintings.epigraph: “The Jews had light, gladness, joy, and honor.”
paintings.poem:
Mordecai walked out
in blue and white
and a crown of gold.

the city that had been perplexed
started shouting.

light,
gladness,
joy,
honor.

four words
where there had been
ashes.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: What single step right in front of you is already lit by His word today, even if the far horizon remains unseen (Esther 8:15–17)?

paintings.title: the other way
paintings.epigraph: “but it was turned out the opposite happened”
paintings.poem:
the day that was chosen
to end them
came.

and it turned
the other way.

they stood together
and were not destroyed.
and the book notes
they left the plunder where it lay.

you can look at the back
of a weaving
and see only knots.

this book lets us
turn it over.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the other way” (Esther 9:1)—where the poem notes, “this book lets us turn it over”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: portions
paintings.epigraph: “sending presents of food to one another, and gifts to the needy.”
paintings.poem:
how do you remember
being rescued?

Mordecai wrote it down:

feast.
be glad.
carry plates of food
to your neighbor's door.

and don't forget
the ones with nothing.

a people once sold
now give things away.

that is how
you know
the sorrow
has really turned.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: How has God quietly provided enough for today’s road, and who might you welcome to your table in kindness (Esther 9:19–22)?

paintings.title: Purim
paintings.epigraph: “Therefore they called these days “Purim”, from the word “Pur.””
paintings.poem:
they named the feast
after the lot
rolled to choose
the day of their ending.

a strange name
for a celebration,
unless the point is:
they are still here.

his name
is never written in this book.

but every year
they tell the story again,

and every year
someone notices
whose hand
was underneath.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: How has God quietly provided enough for today’s road, and who might you welcome to your table in kindness (Esther 9:26–28)?
